column5: waters measured, heavens spanned, mountains weighed
column6: The commentary describes qaddara as fixing quantity and fitting the whole creation; Isaiah asks who has measured the waters, marked off the heavens, and weighed mountains, a concrete creator-and-measure formulation.

column5: ordinances of heaven governing earth
column6: The commentary makes the calculated heavens part of the measure placed in creation; God's interrogation asks whether Job knows the ordinances of heaven or can establish their rule on earth.

column5: declaring the end from the beginning
column6: The commentary defines divine measure by a thing's arrival, essence, and end; Isaiah's God declares the end from the beginning and says the divine purpose will stand.

column5: rain given in its appointed season
column6: The commentary treats rain as descending by measure so that life can emerge; Deuteronomy makes the early and latter rains gifts given to Israel's land in their proper season.

column5: grass supplied for livestock
column6: The commentary's sequence moves from the God who measures and guides to the pasture brought forth for grazing; Deuteronomy has God give grass in the fields for livestock and food for the people.

column5: rain watering earth and making it sprout
column6: The commentary connects measured rain to vegetation's renewal; Isaiah's rain-and-snow image waters the earth and makes it bring forth and sprout, giving seed and bread.

column5: rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness
column6: The commentary reads provision and pasture as the result of a measured created order; Paul names rains from heaven and fruitful seasons as God's witness, filling human hearts with food and gladness.

column5: body clothed with flesh and knit with bones
column6: The commentary gives qaddara the concrete sense of an ordered body gathered in the womb; Job addresses God as the one who clothes him with skin and flesh and knits him with bones and sinews.

column5: formed in the womb for a restoring mission
column6: The commentary joins bodily formation to an assigned direction; Isaiah's servant is formed from the womb in order to bring Jacob back and gather Israel.

column5: just balance and weights as the LORD's work
column6: The commentary says the human-held scale was itself placed by God; Proverbs calls a just balance and scales the LORD's and makes all the weights in the bag God's work.

column5: the servant led in the right way to the bride
column6: The commentary's hidayet imagery includes showing the way to a house and bringing a bride to her husband; Abraham's servant blesses God for leading him in the right way to obtain Rebekah for Isaac.

column5: redeemed people led to a holy habitation
column6: The commentary makes guidance an arrival at the place for which a thing is prepared; the Song of the Sea says God led the redeemed people in steadfast love and guided them to the holy abode.

column5: divine presence going with Moses and giving rest
column6: The commentary stresses that the guide may be beside the traveler, as in Musa's confidence that his Lord is with him; God promises Moses that the divine presence will go with him and give rest.

column5: forty-year wilderness way led by God
column6: The commentary reads Musa's years in Midian and later arrival as a measured journey; Deuteronomy tells Israel to remember the whole wilderness way by which God led them for forty years, testing their response.

column5: teaching wisdom's way and straight paths
column6: The commentary distinguishes a guide's act of showing a road from the traveler's act of walking it; Wisdom says it has taught the way of wisdom and led its pupil in straight paths.

column5: blind led on unknown paths into light
column6: The commentary's guidance is more than a distant sign: it makes a way, levels it, and is associated with light; Isaiah promises to lead the blind by unknown paths, turn darkness to light, and level rough places.

column5: highway where travelers do not go astray
column6: The commentary says one who follows God's guidance does not lose the way; Isaiah's holy highway is described as a way on which travelers, even fools, will not go astray.

column5: straight path by streams without stumbling
column6: The commentary joins guidance, water, and a destination to the image of a gentle leading presence; Jeremiah has God lead the returning people by streams on a straight path where they will not stumble.

column5: a person is led along the chosen way
column6: The commentary says God shows the two ways but the traveler takes or declines one; the Talmud formulates the same relation as the principle that a person is led on the path the person wishes to go.

column5: opening for defilement and help toward purity
column6: The commentary gives a guide's act and the traveler's response distinct roles; this rabbinic maxim says one who comes to defile is given an opening, while one who comes to purify is assisted.

column5: following the light rather than walking in darkness
column6: The commentary unfolds hidayet through fire, light, and the way a traveler actually follows; Jesus identifies himself as the world's light and promises that the follower will not walk in darkness.

column5: Spirit guiding into all truth
column6: The commentary connects the Creator's guidance with revealed instruction and the Prophet's recitation; Jesus says the Spirit of truth will guide the disciples into all truth and disclose what is to come.

column5: straying sheep returned to shepherd and overseer
column6: The commentary sets the person who takes the path against the one who turns aside and repeatedly uses flock imagery; 1 Peter calls its hearers sheep who were straying but have returned to their shepherd and overseer.

column5: humans appointed once to die
column6: The commentary treats measure as a creature's set endpoint rather than only spatial quantity; Hebrews says human beings are appointed to die once and then face judgment.

column5: life and action conditioned by the Lord's will
column6: The commentary contrasts God's measure with the human who thinks and calculates a course independently; James corrects plans for living and acting tomorrow with the formula, If the Lord wills.

column5: set apart from the womb and called by grace
column6: The commentary makes pre-birth formation part of a life placed on a path; Paul describes his own calling as God's setting him apart from his mother's womb and then calling him through grace.

column5: grass clothed today and cast into oven tomorrow
column6: The commentary reads pasture's present flourishing and imminent decay alongside God's provision; Jesus uses grass clothed by God today and thrown into the oven tomorrow to argue for divine care.

column5: blind guides who fall into a pit
column6: The commentary says a would-be guide who still needs guidance cannot rightly lead another; Jesus' warning makes a blind person leading another blind person end with both falling into a pit.

column5: works prepared beforehand as a path to walk
column6: The commentary presents divine preparation as preceding the direction in which a creature moves; Ephesians calls believers God's workmanship, created for good works prepared beforehand so that they may walk in them.

column5: Spirit redirecting an apostolic journey
column6: The commentary gives hidayet its travel sense and says a guide can direct a mission's route; Acts narrates Paul and companions being prevented by the Holy Spirit from speaking in Asia, a concrete redirection on the road.

column5: command not to forget what has been seen
column6: The commentary links Musa's creator-and-guide answer with the surah's following promise of unforgotten recitation; Deuteronomy commands Israel to guard itself, not forget what its eyes have seen, and teach it to descendants.

column5: weighed in balances and found wanting
column6: The commentary contrasts human measuring with the God-given balance that judges it; Daniel's judgment scene weighs Belshazzar in the balances and finds him wanting.

column5: Moses completes a written Torah book
column6: The commentary invokes earlier pages belonging to both Abraham and Moses; Deuteronomy's own closing scene gives a canonical account of Moses finishing the words of Torah in a book, a different scriptural framing of Mosaic writing.
